source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)

coverage.scope: Full In re N.P. Mining opinion; employee §§503/507, income tax §507(a)(8) tests, domestic support, fishermen/grain, deposits, DUI; Problem 5.3(a)-(c) unsolved
coverage.notice: Indexed dollar caps in 2021 textbook are historical, not presented as verified for November 2026.

topics.title: D.2 — In re N.P. Mining: Punitive Fines During Active Postpetition Operation
topics.description: Full Eleventh Circuit case, §959(b) state-law compliance, operation vs passive administration, fine timeline.

entries.title: In re N.P. Mining Co., 963 F.2d 1449 (11th Cir. 1992)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Eleventh Circuit granted admin priority ONLY for penalties attributable to violations occurring during active postpetition operation of the mine by DIP/trustee, subject to prompt assessment filing/notice. Penalties for prepetition violations (even assessed later) and penalties after business stopped and trustee merely administered assets did not qualify. Reversed/remanded.
entries.laymanExplanation: Punitive civil penalties for postpetition legal violations incurred while DIP/trustee actively operates business can qualify as administrative expenses under §503(b)(1)(A), grounded in §959(b); timing of violation and operational status govern, not merely assessment date.
entries.legalExplanation: Kravitch rejected direct benefit, compensatory Reading fairness, or immediate public-health hazard as basis in this record. Instead relied on 28 USC §959(b) that trustee/DIP must operate estate in compliance with valid state law; regulation-related penalties from continuing active mining are costs ordinarily incident to doing business, avoiding unfair competitive advantage of bankrupt coal company. After trustee took control operations ceased (though some brokerage/asset preservation remained), so compliance rationale for MINING operations didn't extend to idle estate; prefiling unremedied violations belong to old bankruptcy liabilities. Claimed ~$2.349m far larger than estate, making priority consequential.
entries.examApplication: Draw 3 phases: active DIP, trustee with mining stopped, Chapter 7 liquidation. Identify when violation occurred (not when fine posted), whether caused by actual estate business operation, and source-era $399,700 vs ~$1.949m amounts.
entries.examTrap: Do NOT say all postpetition fines automatically admin priority, or that a fine assessed after filing for prefiling violation is admin.
entries.sourceRole: Full Eleventh Circuit majority opinion excerpted from uploaded Chapter 5
entries.facts: Alabama Surface Mining Commission enforced strip mine law. N.P. filed Chapter 11 Feb.6,1987 and continued mining as DIP. State assessed $399,700 punitive civil penalties during active DIP operations. Chapter 11 trustee appointed June15,1988 and mining stopped; approximately $1,949,400 additional penalties assessed when only preserving/liquidating assets. Case converted Chapter 7 Apr.14,1989. Commission sought admin priority for about $2.349m noncompensatory penalties, versus estate only $400k–500k. Many fines were attributable to nonabatement of old violations and most not tied to safety/public hazard. Bankruptcy/district courts denied all priority for no direct benefit.
entries.issue: Can purely punitive state environmental civil penalties assessed postpetition be §503(b)(1)(A) administrative expenses despite no estate benefit or compensation to victims, and does active operation versus passive estate administration matter?
entries.holding: Eleventh Circuit granted admin priority ONLY for penalties attributable to violations occurring during active postpetition operation of the mine by DIP/trustee, subject to prompt assessment filing/notice. Penalties for prepetition violations (even assessed later) and penalties after business stopped and trustee merely administered assets did not qualify. Reversed/remanded.
entries.reasoning: Kravitch rejected direct benefit, compensatory Reading fairness, or immediate public-health hazard as basis in this record. Instead relied on 28 USC §959(b) that trustee/DIP must operate estate in compliance with valid state law; regulation-related penalties from continuing active mining are costs ordinarily incident to doing business, avoiding unfair competitive advantage of bankrupt coal company. After trustee took control operations ceased (though some brokerage/asset preservation remained), so compliance rationale for MINING operations didn't extend to idle estate; prefiling unremedied violations belong to old bankruptcy liabilities. Claimed ~$2.349m far larger than estate, making priority consequential.
entries.rule: Punitive civil penalties for postpetition legal violations incurred while DIP/trustee actively operates business can qualify as administrative expenses under §503(b)(1)(A), grounded in §959(b); timing of violation and operational status govern, not merely assessment date.

entries.title: §959(b): trustee/DIP must comply with valid state law while operating
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Federal statute requires bankruptcy estate representative who manages and operates property to obey state laws like other operators; continuing mining cannot ignore pollution rules to save funds.
entries.laymanExplanation: Filing Chapter 11 doesn't give mining company a free competitive advantage by refusing fines.
entries.legalExplanation: Court used §959(b) policy to recognize punitive operating costs as actual/necessary despite no direct estate benefit.
entries.examApplication: For a regulated industry ask if business activity continued after filing and law applied to operation.
entries.examTrap: Does not create same priority for every unpaid prefiling fine.

entries.title: Three phases change legal status
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Active DIP mining (postpetition) can trigger administrative fines for new violations. After trustee takes over and mine operations end, fines from merely maintaining/liquidating estate lack active-operation basis. After Chapter 7 liquidation similarly no mining operations.
entries.laymanExplanation: During mining company works; afterward property simply awaits distribution—different legal function.
entries.legalExplanation: Court looked to substance of operations not generic case title, and trustee moved toward conversion within weeks.
entries.examApplication: Label activity by each time period and violation source.
entries.examTrap: Case not holding that trustee appointment always ends administration priority if business still operates.

entries.title: The dates and amounts are evidence, not interchangeable
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Book reports $399,700 during DIP operating and $1,949,400 later under trustee, total about $2.349m; most claimed penalties occurred when estate couldn't abate violations.
entries.laymanExplanation: Most fines arose after coal mining stopped; priority would exhaust all remaining assets.
entries.legalExplanation: Debtor estate value $400k–500k, hence priority would divert recovery drastically.
entries.examApplication: Calculate which share of assessed fines actually linked to qualifying new operating violations rather than assuming entire first-period total does.
entries.examTrap: Do not automatically award entire $399,700 without separating preexisting violations.

entries.title: Why Reading fairness and Midlantic cleanup didn't control
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: No compensatory victim injury and no identified imminent pollution hazard or cleanup cost in fines. Reading's involuntary harm rationale and Midlantic's public safety abandonment rationale inapplicable; §959(b) active-operation compliance justified narrow result.
entries.laymanExplanation: Punitive fine is not paying harmed victim or cleaning toxic land.
entries.legalExplanation: Distinguish compensatory remedy, actual cleanup costs and penal fines under specific state scheme.
entries.examApplication: For environmental agency assessment identify whether funds improve cleanup or only punish.
entries.examTrap: 'Environmental' label alone doesn't justify administrative priority.

entries.title: No admin priority for prefiling violation assessed later
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Even when agency issues penalty after petition, if violation occurred before filing and simply remains uncorrected, court declined admin cost status under its rationale.
entries.laymanExplanation: Old penalty doesn't become new operating cost because the bill arrives during bankruptcy.
entries.legalExplanation: Case frames estate's fresh beginning and state alternative cessation orders when risks significant.
entries.examApplication: For late fines ask when noncompliance event actually began and what new acts occurred.
entries.examTrap: Don't confuse assessment date with violation date.

entries.title: Case's qualification: prompt proof and notice
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Qualifying operational penalty administrative priority conditional on Commission promptly filing each assessment with bankruptcy court and notifying DIP/trustee.
entries.laymanExplanation: State regulator must formally alert estate to fine instead of silently building massive priority debt.
entries.legalExplanation: This procedural predicate appears in court's express conclusion.
entries.examApplication: Include timing of assessment paperwork/notice in full answer.
entries.examTrap: Cannot claim priority simply from existence of state regulation.

topics.title: D.3(a) — Employee Wage and Benefit Priorities: Timing and Daily Accrual
topics.description: Postpetition administrative wages, prepetition fourth/fifth rank, 180-day windows and source-era limits.

entries.title: Postpetition wages §503(b)(1)(A)(i) administration
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Wages and benefits earned during ongoing estate business operation/postpetition services receive administrative expense status where statutory conditions met; special back-pay §503(b)(1)(A)(ii) also may apply.
entries.laymanExplanation: Employees who work after company files usually aren't stuck in line with old credit card bills.
entries.legalExplanation: Back pay attributable to postpetition unemployment may qualify subject layoff-risk statutory condition.
entries.examApplication: For worker continuing after Chapter 11 filing split wages by service dates.
entries.examTrap: Wages earned before filing don't become admin just because paid afterward.

entries.title: Prepetition wages fourth rank §507(a)(4)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Wages, salaries and commission from services performed within 180 days before earlier petition or cessation of business eligible 4th rank up to indexed per-employee cap, printed $13,650 in book.
entries.laymanExplanation: Workers get extra protection for recent unpaid wages, but not unlimited amounts.
entries.legalExplanation: Separate ordinary allowed balance for earlier wages outside priority window.
entries.examApplication: For 5.3(a) last quarter vacation accrual work timing vs January 1 vesting.
entries.examTrap: Printed $13,650 is historical 2021 indexed figure, not 2026.

entries.title: Benefit contributions fifth rank §507(a)(5)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Unpaid qualifying employee benefit plan contributions for recent 180-day services receive fifth rank subject coordinated cap with individual wage priority.
entries.laymanExplanation: Retirement/health-plan money employer failed to fund is separately protected.
entries.legalExplanation: Temporal and amount limits similar but distinct from wages.
entries.examApplication: List wages and benefit contributions separately and reduce benefit max for certain fourth priority usage.
entries.examTrap: Don't count same worker payment twice.

entries.title: Daily accrual rather than vesting controls 180-day allocation
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: For vacation, severance or sick leave pay, courts presume daily accrual from services rendered even if benefits vest on later date.
entries.laymanExplanation: If leave check becomes payable January 1, employee still earned portions across the year.
entries.legalExplanation: This protects only segment earned in statutory period, and postpetition segment can receive administration rank.
entries.examApplication: For Problem 5.3(a) $2k/year vacation earned before and after Oct1 petition; divide accrual by quarters/days then determine priorities.
entries.examTrap: Do not assign full $2k to whichever date contract says vesting occurs.

entries.title: Policy bases: retention, knowledge disparity, hardship
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Congress protects vulnerable employees, incentivizes workers to remain with struggling enterprise and recognizes workers cannot assess employer credit like sophisticated lenders.
entries.laymanExplanation: Employees are less able to price bankruptcy risk and may flee if wages not protected.
entries.legalExplanation: Justifications support rank but don't override statute caps.
entries.examApplication: Use as rationale in exam policy paragraph.
entries.examTrap: Policy alone won't elevate older wage claim outside 180 days.

topics.title: D.3(b) — Prepetition Tax Priority §507(a)(8) and Postpetition Estate Taxes
topics.description: Three timing pathways for income taxes plus types and discharge consequences.

entries.title: Estate-incurred tax = administrative §503(b)(1)(B),(C)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Tax liability incurred by bankruptcy ESTATE during case usually admin expense at 2nd rank; prepetition tax qualifies for rank 8 only if specific §507(a)(8) category/time window.
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax on estate business after filing is higher priority than owner's old taxes.
entries.legalExplanation: Differentiate debtor personal prepetition tax, estate postpetition operating tax and postcase debtor income.
entries.examApplication: Mark taxable period and legal entity responsible.
entries.examTrap: Don't classify every IRS claim as automatic second rank.

entries.title: §507(a)(8) seven categories share eighth rank
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Includes (A) income/gross receipts, (B) property, (C) withholding, (D) employment, (E) excise, (F) customs, (G) related penalty; no sub-ranking among these tax types.
entries.laymanExplanation: Different old taxes that qualify all share one eighth-priority tier.
entries.legalExplanation: Other temporal predicates vary by tax type and must be checked.
entries.examApplication: First select category, then dates.
entries.examTrap: Don't treat all taxes same or all old taxes entitled to priority.

entries.title: Income-tax 3-year return due test §507(a)(8)(A)(i)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Prepetition income tax qualifies if return (including extensions) was LAST due within three years before filing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax year 2016 return due 2017 may require comparing March2020 petition to 2017 last due date.
entries.legalExplanation: Calculate from legally operative last due (including extensions), not Dec31 tax year end.
entries.examApplication: For 5.3(b) show each relevant exact due date in hypothetical if established, note potential extensions.
entries.examTrap: Don't automatically compute three years from tax-year label.

entries.title: Income-tax 240-day assessment test §507(a)(8)(A)(ii)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Income tax also may qualify if assessed within 240 days before filing, subject applicable statutory suspensions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even older income taxes can be priority if assessed recently.
entries.legalExplanation: Independent route from 3-year return last-due test.
entries.examApplication: Ask assessment date and count back 240 days.
entries.examTrap: Don't assume return filing date equals assessment date.

entries.title: Income-tax assessable after filing §507(a)(8)(A)(iii)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Third independent route covers tax that was not assessed before petition but remained assessable afterward, under statutory conditions.
entries.laymanExplanation: IRS can have priority even before it sends final assessment if law permits later assessment.
entries.legalExplanation: Check status and limitations affecting assessability.
entries.examApplication: If tax return wasn't filed, ask whether tax can still legally be assessed postpetition.
entries.examTrap: Not every unassessed amount qualifies, statute matters.

entries.title: Priority tax is often nondischargeable for individual §523(a)(1)(A)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Qualification for §507(a)(8) also ties to individual debtor discharge exception for listed taxes under §523(a)(1)(A).
entries.laymanExplanation: Some priority tax remains personally collectible after case unless fully paid.
entries.legalExplanation: Other tax nondischargeability routes may apply even without rank 8; source emphasizes dual significance.
entries.examApplication: After ranking tax, separately analyze discharge consequence.
entries.examTrap: Tax has to qualify under applicable rule; don't assume every tax nondischargeable.

topics.title: D.3(c) — Domestic Support, Consumer Deposits, Grain and DUI Injury
topics.description: Special claim eligibility elements, family support subpriority and collection outside stay.

entries.title: Domestic support §101(14A) four-part definition
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Qualifying domestic support owed/recoverable by spouse/former spouse/child/guardian/government, in nature of alimony/maintenance/support, established in divorce/separation/court/admin order and accruing before/on/after relief including interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: Actual support obligation counts regardless of what divorce decree labels it.
entries.legalExplanation: Define based on substance and qualifying payee/order.
entries.examApplication: For 5.3(b) $20k divorce decree support classify nature and rightsholder.
entries.examTrap: Property division that isn't support may not be §101(14A) DSO.

entries.title: Domestic support survives discharge and special collection
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Prepetition DSO §523(a)(5) not discharged even Chapter 13, can reach exempt property §522(c)(1), some proceedings and wage collection excepted §362(b)(2).
entries.laymanExplanation: Bankruptcy cannot simply wipe unpaid child support; support remains due.
entries.legalExplanation: Statutory exceptions differ estate vs nonestate income and by chapter.
entries.examApplication: Analyze case chapter, wage source, stay exception and plan support compliance separately.
entries.examTrap: Do not state all collection from every type of estate asset entirely unrestricted.

entries.title: Support first priority subranking and trustee costs exception
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Direct support owed to spouse/child ranks ahead of assigned-government support within §507(a)(1); limited §507(a)(1)(C) exception for trustee's cost of administering assets otherwise available for support.
entries.laymanExplanation: The family's own unpaid support usually goes ahead of government reimbursement; some trustee costs needed to create fund may come off first.
entries.legalExplanation: States and private support claims not fully identical; eligible plan special treatment government support may vary.
entries.examApplication: When multiple support creditors distinguish family versus state agency.
entries.examTrap: General rule rank1 subject exact statutory implementation.

entries.title: Postpetition DSO payments critical to plan and discharge
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Failure to pay ongoing support can trigger conversion/dismissal, prevent reorganization plan confirmation and Chapter 12/13 discharge certification; ongoing support reduces disposable income calculation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Plan debtor must keep support current as repayment program proceeds.
entries.legalExplanation: Source cites §§1112,1208,1307,1129,1225,1325,1228,1328 and trustee notice duties.
entries.examApplication: In case involving debtor current wages, list support compliance at each case milestone.
entries.examTrap: Claim ranking isn't the only support protection.

entries.title: Grain/fisherman rank6 elements
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Eligible grain producer against storage debtor or U.S. fisher against fish processing/storage debtor, with historical book cap $6,725.
entries.laymanExplanation: A grain farmer whose storage elevator files bankruptcy may recover priority before ordinary trade claims.
entries.legalExplanation: History 1984 farmers forcibly reclaimed grain, prompting targeted statutory policy.
entries.examApplication: Identify creditor profession and business structure; validate cap year.
entries.examTrap: Not general agriculture debt priority.

entries.title: Consumer layaway rank7 elements
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Individual who prepaid for personal/family/household goods or services and never received them can receive priority up to printed source-era indexed $3,025.
entries.laymanExplanation: A gym member prepaid training but gym closed may have priority for unused services.
entries.legalExplanation: Needs actual prefiling deposit, qualifying individual, domestic personal use and undelivered promise.
entries.examApplication: In 5.3(c) prepaid $2k annual personal training; compare delivered vs not delivered between Jan1-Feb1.
entries.examTrap: Not all money paid to failed business is 7th rank.

entries.title: DUI rank10 and discharge exception
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: Nondischargeable death/personal-injury claims caused by unlawful operation of vehicle/vessel while intoxicated receive §507(a)(10) last priority rank.
entries.laymanExplanation: Drunk driver injury victim has special priority even beyond ordinary negligence.
entries.legalExplanation: Separate property damage and normal accident claims from death/personal injury.
entries.examApplication: Check alcohol/drug impairment and unlawful operation facts.
entries.examTrap: Not every DUI fine qualifies this particular civil injury priority.

topics.title: D.3 — Problem 5.3(a)–(c): Priority and Amount (Unsolved)
topics.description: Three original numerical exercises—employee vacation, support/taxes, consumer health club.

entries.title: Separate valuation, tier and actual payout
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
entries.summary: For each scenario identify original claim dollar amount; cap or accrued part eligible for priority; rank; unencumbered fund; then calculate payment only if higher classes satisfied and facts suffice.
entries.laymanExplanation: Eligible special claim may still go unpaid when earlier rank consumes the estate.
entries.legalExplanation: Do not misread 2021 caps as current, and don't invent missing 2016 assessment/extension facts.
entries.examApplication: Keep separate statutory eligibility from order of distribution.
entries.examTrap: Problems remain unanswered for independent attempt.

problems.title: Problem 5.3(a)
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
problems.prompt: Worker had $2,000 vacation pay claim earned over one year's service, vested at beginning of calendar year. Debtor filed Chapter 11 October 1 (start Q4); worker stayed employed until next Jan1 vesting. Analyze split across prefiling fourth-priority 180-day window and postfiling administrative wage category, and limits. No solution.

problems.title: Problem 5.3(b)
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
problems.prompt: Debtor owes $14,000 income tax for 2016; divorce in 2017 gave former spouse $20,000 support; Chapter 7 filing March 1, 2020; only $22,000 nonexempt unencumbered assets. Identify taxes' eligibility under §507(a)(8) using actual due/assessment facts and rank1 support; compute distribution if supported. Leave original problem unanswered.

problems.title: Problem 5.3(c)
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 5 §D.2 In re N.P. Mining full opinion and §D.3 Other Priorities, Problem 5.3(a)-(c)
problems.prompt: Consumer Jan1 paid $2,000 deposit for one year personal training at Debtor Health Club; Feb1 club closed and filed Chapter 7. Assess §507(a)(7) eligibility, delivered vs undelivered portion and extent of priority. Leave unanswered.
